Data sources



Source
What it has
Format
Used for




PATH Ridership Statistics, Port Authority of NY & NJ
Monthly reports (2012–present) and hourly reports (2017–present, plus Jul 2014 and Nov 2016 snapshots), by station
PDF only: no API, no CSV
Main source for all charts


FTA National Transit Database: Complete Monthly Ridership (PATH = NTD ID 20098) · NTD monthly ridership page
Monthly system-wide unlinked trips, 2002–present
CSV / API
Cross-check


NY Open Data: PATH Monthly Ridership, Beginning 1996 (data.gov listing)
Monthly system total in thousands. Stopped updating in 2016
CSV / API
Cross-check


NY Open Data: PATH Average Weekday & Weekend Ridership, Beginning 1996 (data.gov listing)
Average weekday and weekend ridership, system total. Stopped in 2016
CSV / API

APTA Quarterly Ridership Reports (archive)
Quarterly unlinked trips by agency (listed as “Port Authority of NY & NJ”, heavy rail)
PDF
Not used (quarterly, system only)



Why PDFs, when there are CSVs? The two free machine-readable sources don’t cover what this project needs. NY Open Data stopped in 2016. The National Transit Database is current but has system totals only, with no stations and no hours. The Port Authority’s PDFs are the only source with station-level and hourly detail up to the present. So the PDFs are the main source, and the CSV/API sources are used to check them.
The PDFs live at https://www.panynj.gov/content/dam/path/about/statistics/<file>.pdf. File names vary by year (2012_PATH_Ridership_Report, 2015-PATH-Ridership-Report, …-hourly-… vs …-Hourly-…), so scripts/01_download.py lists each one explicitly.

title: PATH ridership: methodology & data
text:
Pipeline: step by step









Step
Script / file
Input → output
What it does




1. Download
scripts/01_download.py
PANYNJ, NY Open Data and NTD URLs → data/raw/
Downloads 15 monthly and 12 hourly PDF reports, plus the two CSV/API sources. Checks each PDF is valid and skips files already on disk.


2. Parse monthly
scripts/02_parse_monthly.py
data/raw/pdf/monthly_*.pdf → data/processed/path_monthly_by_station.csv, path_monthly_system.csv, crosscheck_system_totals.csv
Reads the PDF text layer (pdfplumber), finds each month’s page, extracts both station tables and the day-count row, standardises station names, validates, and compares with NY Open Data and NTD.


3. Parse hourly
scripts/03_parse_hourly.py
data/raw/pdf/hourly_*.pdf → data/processed/path_hourly.csv, hourly_parse_issues.csv
Reads every station page (section label, station, 24 hours × 8 columns) and reshapes it to a long “tidy” table. Any row it can’t parse is logged.


4. Charts
pathviz.py
processed CSVs → Plotly figures
One module defines every chart, so the dashboard and the presentation always match.


5. Publish
path/dashboard.qmd, path/slides.qmd, _quarto.yml
→ website (_site/)
Quarto renders the dashboard, slides and this page. GitHub Pages hosts them.



python scripts/01_download.py      # step 1
python scripts/02_parse_monthly.py # step 2
python scripts/03_parse_hourly.py  # step 3
quarto render                      # steps 4–5

Problems the parser handles

Two tables per page. Each station appears twice on a monthly page: first as totals and averages, then as average-daily and totals by day type. The parser tells them apart by order.
Renamed stations. “Pavonia/ Newport” → “Newport”, “WTC” → “World Trade Center”, “Christopher St.” → “Christopher Street”.
Section labels change format across years (“January 2021”, “Jun 2025”, “2026-Jan”, “YTD 2019”, “2025 Annual”), and ASCII and Unicode hyphens are mixed.
Blank holiday columns in months with no holiday (e.g. Mar, Apr and Aug 2026) leave 6 values per row instead of 8.
One-off snapshot reports (July 2014, November 2016) use slightly different headers.
macOS file names are case-insensitive, so Hourly.pdf and hourly.pdf would overwrite each other. Files are saved as hourly_2025.pdf etc.

title: PATH ridership: methodology & data
text:
Data definitions
What is counted. Every number comes from PATH’s faregates, the turnstiles and TAPP gates riders pass through. There are two kinds of count:









Term
What it means
Which station it describes
Where it’s used




Entry (also “trip” or “ridership”)
A person passing into the system through a faregate
The origin: the station where the trip starts
Monthly data (all charts on the Overview and Monthly pages), and the hourly charts unless marked “exits”


Exit
A person passing out through a faregate
The destination: the station where the trip ends
Hourly data only, where marked



Example: someone who commutes from Hoboken to 33rd Street and back counts as an entry at Hoboken in the morning and an entry at 33rd Street in the evening. That’s two trips. Their morning exit is counted at 33rd Street.
How exits are counted. PATH riders tap in only. Nobody taps out, so exits don’t come from fare payments. The hourly reports are labelled “Turnstile Count” (through 2023) and “Legacy and TAPP Faregates Count” (from 2024). Exits are the number of people physically passing out through the exit turnstiles or faregates, and the gate counts each passage without charging. Because entries and exits aren’t linked to a card, the data can’t say where a particular rider went. There are no origin–destination pairs, only how many trips started and ended at each station.
Entries vs. exits don’t match system-wide after 2021. Through 2019, system-wide weekday exits were within about 1% of entries, as expected. Since 2022 exits have run about 9–12% higher than entries. The reports don’t explain this. Possible reasons include entries that aren’t counted (cross-honor, freewheeled, fare evasion) and differences between the old and new gates. For this reason the dashboard uses entries for all ridership totals, and uses exits only to show when trips end.
Other terms

Average weekday / Saturday / Sunday / holiday. Total entries on that type of day, divided by the number of those days in the month. Holidays are days PATH runs a holiday schedule, and they’re left out of the weekday, Saturday and Sunday averages.
Rush hours. In this project: 7–9 am and 5–7 pm (four one-hour periods).
Cross-honor. Tickets from other operators (e.g. NJ Transit) that PATH accepts during service disruptions. These are not included in the counts.
Freewheeled entries. Excluded from 2024 on, per the report headers. The reports don’t define the term. It usually means gates set to free entry, with no fare charged.
Legacy + TAPP. From 2023, counts combine the old turnstiles and PATH’s new contactless TAPP faregates.
Linked vs. unlinked trips. The PATH reports count linked trips: one faregate entry per journey, even if the rider changes trains. The federal National Transit Database counts unlinked trips, meaning every boarding, so a transfer counts twice. That’s why NTD totals run about 6–11% higher than the PATH reports every month.

title: PATH ridership: methodology & data
text:
Limitations

Faregate entries are not unique people. A daily commuter makes about 40 trips a month. Fare evasion, cross-honored and freewheeled entries are not counted.
Closures show up as near-zero values, not as missing data. Examples: WTC and Exchange Place weekends in much of 2014, Hoboken in February 2025 (about 2,700 a weekday and zero on weekends), and low WTC weekend values in 2019. They’re real counts, but they pull averages down.
Hourly data starts in 2017, plus one-month snapshots for July 2014 and November 2016. Exits are only available in the hourly data.
The current year is partial (through the latest published month).
Fare-system change. The move from old turnstiles to TAPP faregates (2023–25) changed the counting equipment. Small shifts in that period may partly reflect measurement.
Rounding. The PDFs round averages to whole people, so sums of hourly values can be off by a few.

text: Hi, I’m AP. I’m a data analyst who likes taking messy public data and turning it into something people can explore. Each project below has an interactive dashboard, a short presentation of the findings, and a methodology page covering sources, definitions and limitations.

title: Data Projects Portfolio
text:
Projects

PATH train ridership, 2012–2026
The Port Authority publishes PATH ridership only as PDF reports, with no API or CSV. I built a pipeline that extracts 15 years of monthly and hourly data from 27 reports (over 2,000 pages). It validates the results against the reports’ own subtotals and two government datasets. The analysis covers how ridership collapsed in 2020, how it has recovered, and how the daily commute changed.

title: PATH ridership, 2012–2026
text:
The question
PATH links Newark, Harrison, Jersey City and Hoboken with Manhattan. It has 13 stations and carried about 280,000 riders a weekday before 2020.


What happened to PATH ridership?

How deep was the 2020 collapse?
How far has it recovered?
Has the shape of the commute changed?


The catch: no usable data
The Port Authority publishes ridership only as PDFs, with no API and no CSV. The free datasets either stopped in 2016 (NY Open Data) or have no station or hourly detail (National Transit Database).

title: PATH ridership, 2012–2026
text:
What I built


1 · Extract
Downloaded 27 PDF reports (more than 2,000 pages) and parsed every table with Python (pdfplumber).

2 · Validate
Every month’s stations add up exactly to the printed totals. The results match NY Open Data within 0.33%, and their movements track the federal NTD.

3 · Publish
Clean CSVs, an interactive dashboard and these slides, all from one shared chart module so the numbers always match.








Reading the numbers


A trip = one person entering through a faregate, counted at the station where the trip starts. Exits (where trips end) appear only in the hourly data.

Limitations

Entries ≠ people. A daily commuter makes about 40 trips a month, and cross-honored and freewheeled entries are excluded.
Closures look like near-zero values (e.g. Hoboken, Feb 2025), not missing data.
Hourly detail starts in 2017, plus two one-month snapshots (2014, 2016).
Fare-system change (TAPP, 2023–25) altered the counting equipment.
